bib.title: Re-examining Whether, Why, and How Human-AI Interaction Is Uniquely Difficult to Design

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Re-examining Whether, Why, and How Human-AI Interaction Is Uniquely Difficult to Design", Qian Yang, Aaron Steinfeld, Carolyn Rose, John Zimmerman (Carnegie Mellon University). CHI 2020, April 25-30, Honolulu (Paper 174). ACM ISBN 978-1-4503-6708-0/20/04. DOI printed: http://dx.doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376301. No arXiv id in the text. CC BY 4.0.

COVERAGE: Pages 1-13 of 13; extraction was 67,564 chars. I read chars 0-58,500 in full: abstract, related work, method, framework, using the framework, conclusion, and refs 1-32. I skipped the rest of the reference list because it only holds origins. Figure 5 is an image, so I rendered page 9 and read it visually.

IDENTITY CHECK against references.md line 79:
- Authors, "Yang et al.", CHI 2020 and title are all correct.
- DOI 10.1145/3313831.3376301 matches the printed DOI.
- Venue is correct.
- "Capability uncertainty and output complexity, four levels" is accurate.
- Caution: this is Qian Yang, not the Yang of SWE-agent. notes/04-coding-agent.md cites a different "Yang et al." (arXiv 2405.15793, NeurIPS 2024), so a bare "Yang et al." is ambiguous across notes.
- Notes citing this paper: only notes/06-application-patterns.md line 141. It says Yang et al. "explain why this is hard: AI design differs because of uncertainty about what the system can do and the complexity of its outputs, and they place systems on four levels along those two axes (CHI 2020)... That is why failures are so hard to prototype before the system exists." That is consistent with the paper. The note never names the levels.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Claim: Two sources make AI distinctly hard to design: capability uncertainty and output complexity.
 number: 2 sources, 4 levels
 setup: conceptual framework synthesized from the authors' own cases; not empirically tested.
 quote: "We identify two sources of AI's distinctive design challenges: 1) uncertainty surrounding AI's capabilities, 2) AI's output complexity, spanning from simple to adaptive complex. We identify four levels of AI systems. On each level, designers encounter a different subset of the design challenges."
 where: p1, abstract
2. Claim: Definitions of the two dimensions.
 number: none
 setup: both are continua
 quote: "capability uncertainty (uncertainties surrounding what the system can do and how well it performs) and output complexity (complexity of the outputs that the system might generate). Both dimensions function along a continuum."
 where: p6
3. Claim: Output complexity, not unpredictability, is the root cause. A random-word bot is unpredictable but easy to simulate; Siri is quasi-random and resists simulation.
 number: none
 setup: argued by example, not tested
 quote: "Notably, output complexity is not output unpredictability. While prior research often viewed AI systems' unpredictable errors as causing UX troubles, we argue that AI's output complexity is the root cause."
 where: p7
4. Claim: The four levels (Figure 5, p9; text covers only levels 1 and 4).
 - Level 1, Probabilistic Systems: learn from a self-contained dataset, small fixed output set. Examples: face detection, adaptive menus, toxicity detectors. Existing HCI methods suffice.
   quote: "Level one systems learn from a self-contained dataset. They produce a small, fixed set of outputs."
 - Level 2, Adaptive Systems (figure only): outputs adaptive to user profile and use contexts, but no post-deployment learning. Figure labels it "Designing Adaptive Interactions at scale (due to output complexity)". The text gives no level-2 example in prose, only that rule-based simulators work for level 2 "systems that generate a broad set of outputs".
 - Level 3, Evolving Probabilistic Systems (figure only): performance fluctuates and diversifies with unseen data, outputs probabilistic. Figure labels it "Designing User-System Co-evolvement (due to capability uncertainty)".
 - Level 4, Evolving Adaptive Systems: both.
   quote: "Level four systems learn from new data even after deployment. They also produce adaptive, open-ended outputs that resist abstraction. Search engines, newsfeed rankers, automated email replies, a recommender system that suggests 'items you might like,' would all fit in this category."
 - Level 4 is a superset: "The design challenges of Level 4 are also a superset of issues encountered in Levels 2 and 3."
 where: p8-9
5. Claim: Rule-based simulators help for levels 1-2 and fail for levels 3-4.
 number: levels 1-2 vs 3-4
 quote: "rule-based simulators are most effective in prototyping level 1-2 systems... However, rule-based simulators cannot easily prototype systems that autonomously learn from user-generated data (level 3-4)."
 where: p10
6. Claim: Level 1 has none of the four design challenges. Level 4 has all four: understanding capabilities, envisioning, iterative prototyping, collaborating with engineers.
 quote: "Existing HCI sketching and prototyping methods can sufficiently cover level one systems, systems with known capability with few possible outputs."
 where: p8
7. Claim: Capability uncertainty persists after deployment; performance can drift.
 quote: "The performance of a deployed AI system can constantly fluctuate and diverge when it gains new data to improve its learning." Also: "the system's performance improves for users and use contexts that have produced rich data. It performs worse for less frequent users and less typical situations."
 where: p6-7
8. Claim: The two common ways to prototype AI both fail. Wizard of Oz or rule-based simulators cannot simulate inference errors; field trials lose rapid iteration.
 quote: "this approach fails to address any of the UX issues that will come from AI inference errors because there is no way to simulate these errors"
 where: p3
9. Claim: Related work has no empirical evaluation of proposed AI design tools.
 quote: "we found no empirical evaluations of the proposed design tools, guidelines, or workflows."
 where: p4
10. Claim: Yang critiques Amershi et al. (CHI 2019) guidelines as not AI-specific.
 quote: "These seem important to AI systems, but they also seem to be issues that designers must address in systems with no AI."
 where: p4

METHOD (numbers)
- Not a controlled study. The authors curated "a set of human-AI interaction sketching and prototyping processes as case studies" from their own research, design and teaching, and re-analyzed data from projects published at DIS and CHI (teaching excluded).
- Own design work: simple adaptive UIs, crowd-sourced transportation systems, clinical decision support, NL productivity tools.
- Practitioner study 1: "We interviewed 14 product designers/managers and surveyed 98 more... We also interviewed the 10 professional AI engineers".
- Practitioner study 2: "We interviewed 13 designers who had designed AI applications for many, many years".
- Teaching: day-long Designing AI workshops, one instructor with 2-3 students, "26 HCI Master students from two universities"; plus a one-semester studio course, "Approximately 40 undergraduate and master students".
- Analysis: affinity diagramming. "We proposed and discussed more than 50 thematic constructs and frameworks." Participants were the three authors, an external faculty member and an industry researcher, each with at least 5 years of AI and HCI research. Critique sessions: a research group of "about 40 HCI researchers" and one of "12 machine learning researchers". Criteria: analytical leverage, explanatory power, constructive potential.
- AI definition used (Kaplan & Haenlein 2019): "computational systems that interpret external data, learn from such data, and use those learnings to achieve specific goals and tasks through flexible adaptation." They also included expert systems and crowd-sourcing in the analysis.

LIMITS: The authors concede: "the case studies are mainly from our own research/design/teaching experiences. This is neither a representative sample nor a comprehensive one." The framework is "a moderate first step" and the authors "encourage fellow researchers to critique, evaluate, and improve" it. It is not validated. The paper pre-dates LLMs and agents (2020). Its examples are Siri, recommenders, face tagging and toxicity classifiers. Output complexity in the open-ended sense plausibly applies to LLMs, but the paper does not say so. The text describes levels 1 and 4 only; levels 2 and 3 appear in Figure 5 and in one sentence on simulators. The text states no counts of designers per level and no outcome metrics.

BUILDS ON: Dove et al. 2017 (UX Design Innovation: ML as a design material); Amershi et al. 2019 (Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction); Holmquist 2017 (AI as a design material); Bly & Churchill 1999 (design through matchmaking); Kaplan & Haenlein 2019 (AI definition); Girardin & Lathia 2017; Yang et al. own prior work (refs [52-60]); Double Diamond (Design Council 2005); Wizard-of-Oz tools (Klemmer 2000, Suede).

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 5 (p9): Four levels of AI systems according to design complexity. This is the quickest way to see the levels. Rows are Level 1 Probabilistic, Level 2 Adaptive, Level 3 Evolving Probabilistic, Level 4 Evolving Adaptive. Level 3 and 4 add a "Deployed System Performance Over Time" step (capability uncertainty). Level 2 and 4 add "outputs adaptive to user profile and use contexts" (output complexity).
- Fig 3 (p7): the pathway from algorithm capability to user experience, with the extra steps from capability uncertainty and output complexity.
- Fig 4 (p8): "The AI design complexity map" (two-axis map; not read as an image).
- Fig 1, 2 (p2-3): challenges mapped onto Double Diamond and MVP processes. Fig 6 (p10): the framework applied to AI fairness.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Text extraction was clean, with ligature and hyphen artifacts only. Levels 2 and 3 come only from the Figure 5 image, which I read visually. The PDF metadata carries a 2025 modification date (an iText re-save), which does not change the content. Minor: reference [29] and [30] are duplicates in the paper's own list.
